# Verification Strategy

Manual test cases are often written the way a human would check them, not
the way a script can. "Order is placed successfully" is a valid expected
result for a person clicking through the app; it is not, by itself,
something `script-generator` can turn into an `expect()` call. This skill
is what `step-parser` and `script-generator` both apply to close that gap -
the requirement-level question of *what actually proves this step worked*,
before assertion-strategy decides how to write it in code.

## Turning a vague expected result into a checkable signal

For every expected result, identify at least one concrete, observable
signal - and prefer more than one when the DSL step implies it:

- **UI signal** - a confirmation message, a new element appearing, a
  navigation to a new URL/route, a field's value changing.
- **State signal** - a button becoming enabled/disabled, a status badge
  changing, an item appearing in a list that didn't have it before.
- **Persistence signal** - reloading the page (or navigating away and back)
  and confirming the change survived, when the DSL result implies something
  was saved, not just displayed.

If `step-parser` cannot identify at least one concrete signal for an
expected result, it should not silently guess one - flag it in the
`.dsl.notes.md` file (per the dsl-governance skill) as needing SME
clarification, per item 6.3's human-in-the-loop checkpoint, rather than
letting an unverifiable step reach `script-generator`.

## Multi-signal outcomes

When a step's real-world outcome has more than one observable consequence
(an order confirmation page appears *and* the cart badge clears *and* an
email would be sent), verify the signals the test can actually observe in
this run (the first two) and note the ones it can't (email delivery) as an
explicit, acknowledged gap in the generated test's comments - not a silent
omission. A reviewer should be able to tell "we didn't check this" from
"we checked this and it's covered."

## Traceability to acceptance criteria

Where the source test case traces back to a user story with acceptance
criteria (item 6.4's traceability model), the verification signal should
map directly to language in that acceptance criterion. If it doesn't - if
the acceptance criteria says one thing and the only observable signal
proves something narrower - that mismatch is worth surfacing explicitly
rather than quietly verifying the narrower thing and calling the step done.

## When this needs to change

A recurring pattern of `verification-strategy` corrections - for example,
DSL files repeatedly reaching `script-generator` with expected results that
turn out to be unverifiable as stated - is a signal to tighten
`step-parser`'s guidance here, not just to keep patching individual DSL
files by hand. Log it, and let `skill-curator` fold the pattern back into
this skill.

## Learned patterns

Read [references/learned-patterns.md](./references/learned-patterns.md) when deciding what a step must verify. It holds verifications engineers added after actions that change the page - fixes that recurred across several files and engineers and were approved by a reviewer (generated by `npm run learn-publish`; do not edit it by hand). Treat it as part of this skill.

If you hit a problem it does not cover, run `npm run lookup-fix -- "<problem>"`. After you fix it by hand, record the fix with `npm run learn-capture -- --worktree --write --why "<what was wrong>"` so it can become a pattern (see the **fix-knowledge-base** skill).
